kernelIdea: The complement of S ∩ T is S̄ ∪ T̄, and the complement of S ∪ T is S̄ ∩ T̄. These are the logic laws of 1.4 with ¬ ↔ complement, ∧ ↔ ∩, ∨ ↔ ∪.

kernels.l1: Outside both hoops is the same as outside this one and outside that one.
kernels.l2: The outside of the overlap is the outside of one hoop joined with the outside of the other. The outside of both hoops together is where the two outsides overlap.
kernels.l3: Everything outside an overlap is the same as everything outside the first pooled with everything outside the second — and the same swap works the other way round.
kernels.l4: The complement of an intersection is the union of the complements, and the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements. These are De Morgan's logic laws with complement for *not*.
kernels.l5: Taking complements exchanges intersection with union. Each law is proved by double inclusion, with the logic law of §1.4 doing the work at the pivot.
kernels.l6: Taking complements swaps intersection with union and reverses containment. These are Chapter 1's De Morgan laws carried over to sets, with the same proof underneath.
kernels.l7: Complementation exchanges intersection and union in both directions. The proof is a double inclusion whose pivot step is the logic law of §1.4.
kernels.l8: De Morgan for sets is the same identity as for connectives, because P(X) and the two-element Boolean algebra satisfy the same equational theory; the laws extend verbatim to indexed families via ¬∀ ≡ ∃¬.
